properties.chose: Built as ONE skill, `why` (/why), with two walks — by feature and by change — separate from adopt, with adopt pointing to it (the hub agent's recommendation, option (f)). Order is chosen by the owner at setup, led by 'what would an agent get wrong' (a); pages of changes answered in one message (b); noise and churn triage scripted (c); resumable through a `why_cursor` finding per feature (d); other people's changes become follow-ups naming them (e). The payoff — delivering a feature's reasons before an agent edits a file — is not built.
properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony, 2026-09-23, following Alex's feedback (dec:idea-adopt-can-be-an-intent-interview-that-records-the-why-and-where-and-skips-the-structure).

HIS WORDS: "can we maybe make a skill that sees how a design has changed from its commit history, then systematically go through those changes with the user to see why they added a feature or moved a button or changed its functionality in some way? The commit history should show what changed — I think what my brother is getting at is 'why they made a change?' Obviously, this would be for design projects that have commit history only. Maybe call it '/change-justification'… the skill would go through a repo's commit history and capture all changes via commit history, then systematically go through each change with the user to ask why the change was made. Sometimes it isn't clear from the commit message why somebody changed something."

⭐⭐ THE SPLIT THAT MAKES IT WORK, and it squares with Alex's "the commit history does not have the context I want to provide": the history is used ONLY as the index of WHAT changed and WHEN, never as the source of WHY. The why comes from a person, which is exactly what dec:idea-should-the-server-journal-every-write-itself says no automatic journal can supply. Alex's interview asks "why does this feature EXIST?"; this asks "why did it CHANGE?" — two walks over the same intent, one present-tense, one historical.

THE LOOP, as proposed:
  1. Read the history (git log with file lists and stats; the diff itself only when the summary is not enough).
  2. Group commits into CHANGES a person would recognise (a PR, a feature's run of commits), and drop the noise (formatting, dependency bumps, CI, typo fixes, bots).
  3. For each change, say in plain words what changed ("the export button moved from the toolbar to the File menu"), when and by whom, the commit message, and — via tools/impact_of_diff.py, which already maps a commit range to the capabilities and requirements its files serve — which part of the design it touched.
  4. Ask why, offering the agent's best reading of the message; accept "don't know", "skip", "same as #12".
  5. Record the answer: a ChangeEvent dated at the commit (detected_at), what in `summary`, why in `rationale`, CHANGED edges to what it touched; plus a Requirement (with `source` = the user or profile who needed it) when the answer names a need, or a Decision when it names a choice.

OPTIONS WITHIN IT, NONE CHOSEN:

(a) ORDER. Newest first (memory is freshest, and recent changes matter most to today's code); oldest first (the story in order, so later answers can cite earlier ones); or BY FEATURE — every change to one feature together, so "why is it like this now" builds up in one place. By-feature fits "why did they move the button" best.

(b) BATCHING. Ten to twenty changes per page with the agent's guesses, answered in one message. The same device as Alex's interview option (b).

(c) TRIAGE, because six years is thousands of commits: user-visible changes first (screens, routes, exports), then reverts (a revert always has a reason), large or high-churn changes, and anything the commit message leaves unexplained. Report coverage honestly: "asked about 140 of 2,300 changes; the rest were grouped, skipped as noise, or deferred".

(d) RESUMABLE, like adopt's region mode: a cursor for the last change reviewed, and a deferral marker for changes skipped, so a session picks up where the last one stopped.

(e) OTHER PEOPLE'S CHANGES. When the owner doesn't know why a colleague changed something, the question is recorded for that person (the commit author) rather than guessed.

(f) ONE SKILL OR TWO. A single skill with two walks (by feature for "why does it exist", by change for "why did it change"), or this as a sibling of Alex's intent interview.

THE HONEST COUNTER-ARGUMENTS, recorded beside the idea:
· MEMORY IS A RECONSTRUCTION. An answer given years later is not a contemporaneous record. The record should say so (recalled, when, by whom, how sure), or a recalled reason will read with the authority of one written at the time. reflow2 has no "recalled" marker on a ChangeEvent today.
· COMMITS ARE THE WRONG UNIT surprisingly often: squash-merges hide the steps, rebases rewrite them, one commit can hold three unrelated changes, and a feature can take forty commits. Grouping is where most of the judgement sits.
· COST. Reading diffs is expensive; file lists and stats first, diffs on demand. The owner's time is the scarcer resource, and triage matters more than completeness.
· BACKWARD RECORDS AND FORWARD RULES. dec:the-cause-discipline-binds-forward-not-backward says a discipline binds from when it exists, not before. Historical ChangeEvents should not raise the checks written for new work (a "fix without a recorded cause" alarm on a 2021 bug fix is noise), so they need to be recognisable as historical.
· ONLY FOR PROJECTS WITH HISTORY, as Anthony said; and only as good as the history's granularity.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
SHARPENED 2026-09-23 — WHERE IT SITS AGAINST ADOPT, WHAT IT RECOVERS, AND ITS NAME
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

⭐⭐ ANTHONY'S FRAMING, which says what this skill is FOR better than anything above. His words: "the design process is: concept --> decisions/requirements --> implemented design --> fielded or operational (that is probably abbreviated version). When we use adopt, we are getting the 'what' the design is implemented design --> fielded or operational (I think I even designed the adopt skill using reverse engineering processes). In the adopt skill, you are missing the 'concept --> decisions/requirements' phases and in a true reverse engineering process, you may not ever get those. In the case of my brother, we have the commit history and his memory for 'concept --> decisions/requirements' phase. So this is kind of doing reverse engineering where you have the design lead telling you why they made all the decisions that you now see as implemented/fielded. This is kind of like in my past job when we had an old piece of technology and had to bring some guy out of retirement to fix the old system (because he was the only one that knew how the system worked)."

  ⇒ THE TWO SKILLS RECOVER OPPOSITE HALVES OF THE SAME CHAIN (the founding chain in dec:idea-design-is-composable-on-two-axes-authority-and-role: concept → requirements → capabilities → verified → fielded).
    · ADOPT recovers the BACK half — implemented and fielded — from the artifact, by reverse engineering (redocumentation plus design recovery). Its own text concedes the front half: intent "comes from everywhere else, or from the user", and a true reverse-engineering effort may never get it.
    · THIS SKILL recovers the FRONT half — concept, decisions, requirements — from the one source that holds it: the person who made them. It is reverse engineering WITH the design lead in the room. Anthony's retiree is the canonical case: the system is fully present and nobody left can say why it is the way it is.
  ⇒ It is KNOWLEDGE ELICITATION, not code analysis. The commit history (and, for the feature walk, the code) only sets the agenda; every answer is the person's word, recorded as recalled.
  ⇒ AND IT HAS A DEADLINE THE CODE DOES NOT: the code will still be there next year, and the person may not be. That is an argument for doing the highest-value questions first (triage, option (c)), not for completeness.

⭐ RECOMMENDATION (the dev_reflow2 hub agent's, 2026-09-23; a finding, NOT a decision — Anthony asked for it to be recorded as a recommendation): SEPARATE FROM ADOPT, WITH ADOPT POINTING TO IT; NEITHER A REPLACEMENT NOR A NEW PHASE OF ADOPT.
  · NOT A REPLACEMENT: adopt answers a different question (what exists, under design control) and works where there is no git history and no person to ask (drawings, devices, systems whose designers are gone). Projects that need the structural half still need it.
  · NOT A PHASE OF ADOPT, for three reasons. (1) A skill is found by its own description; Alex never reached adopt, and a separate skill whose description reads "record why the code is the way it is / why it changed" is found by exactly the request that needs it. (2) Adopt is a one-time onboarding act; this runs repeatedly — after any stretch of work, on projects started with genesis too (flo2 once rebuilt two days of change history from git a day late). (3) Adopt is already long and structure-first, which is the opposite order from the one this needs.
  · THE LINKS BETWEEN THEM, all light: (i) adopt's intent-recovery step (Phase 3) gains one line — where the project has history and its design lead is available, run this skill for the why; (ii) adopt asks its purpose first (option (e) of dec:idea-adopt-can-be-an-intent-interview-that-records-the-why-and-where-and-skips-the-structure): "controlling the structure, or keeping the why?", and the second answer routes here; (iii) ALEX'S FEATURE INTERVIEW AND THIS BECOME ONE SKILL WITH TWO WALKS — by feature ("why does this exist?", the present) and by change ("why did it change?", the history). Both are interviews of the same person, record the same shapes (a need with its user as source, a decision, a dated change with its reason) and need the same machinery (batching, triage, resuming, recall marked as recall).
  · So the family would be three: GENESIS (forward, from a concept), ADOPT (backward, the implemented and fielded half), and this (backward, the concept and decision half, from the people who hold it).

📌 NAME: Anthony finds `/change-justification` too long and suggests `/why` or `/the-why`. With the two walks merged, `/why` names both ("why does this exist", "why did it change") and is the shortest; `/the-why` reads better in prose. Not chosen here. Whichever it is must be checked against the served skill names and their slash shortcuts when it is built.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
SHARPENED 2026-09-23 — A WALKTHROUGH: HOW A DESIGN LEAD USES /why ON A HUGE, OLD CODEBASE
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING. Anthony asked for the walkthrough of someone like Alex (six years, ~10k hours, thousands of commits, agents that already navigate the code well) actually using it. Illustrative numbers throughout; nothing here was measured.

── SESSION 0: SET UP (about 15 minutes of his time) ──
1. HE SAYS WHAT IT'S FOR. The skill asks four things and records them as one project-level decision: which repos or areas are in scope; who the design lead is (him) and who else holds history; how long a session he'll give (say 30 minutes); and what matters most right now (a part being rewritten, what auditors ask about, what new staff break).
2. A MECHANICAL PASS, NEARLY FREE. Scripts, not the model, read git: the log with authors, dates, file lists and line counts. They group commits into CHANGES (by PR or merge, else by branch, author, time window and files), drop the noise by rule (bots, dependency bumps, formatting, CI), flag reverts, and count churn per area. Output, e.g.: "2,300 commits → 640 changes; 180 user-visible; 25 reverts; the 20 most-changed areas".
3. A FEATURE LIST IN HIS WORDS. One shallow agent pass over the user-facing surface only (routes, screens, menus, exports, reports) proposes a feature inventory; he renames and prunes it in one reply. This is the only broad reading of code, and it is shallow on purpose.
4. HE PICKS THE ORDER. The skill proposes an order from the signals — ⭐ led by "WHAT WOULD AN AGENT GET WRONG?": code that looks unnecessary or odd but is deliberate (the Chesterton's-fence cases), where a capable agent would "clean it up" and break something. That is the history with the highest value per minute, and it is exactly what Alex's agents cannot deduce. Then reverts, then the most-changed user-visible features.

── SESSIONS 1..N: THE LOOP (30–45 minutes each, one feature at a time) ──
5. TODAY'S FEATURE, e.g. "Report export — 37 changes since 2019".
6. PAGE 1, WHY IT EXISTS (the feature walk). The agent states what it sees ("an export button on the results screen producing PDF and CSV") and asks who needed it. His answer ("auditors needed CSV for their spreadsheets; the PDF is for the monthly board pack") lands as: the capability (built, where it lives: one directory), two needs each with its user as source, the links between them — his word, so accepted with him as approver.
7. PAGE 2, WHY IT CHANGED (the history walk). The feature's grouped changes as a numbered timeline, one line each: date, author, message, the agent's guess.
     2  2020-07  moved export button toolbar → File menu   guess: ?
     3  2021-01  revert "store export timestamps in local time"   guess: timezone bug?
     9  2023-04  (Maria) split CSV into two files   guess: ?
   He answers the page in ONE message: "2: people hit it by accident when printing. 3: the auditors' system assumes UTC. 5–8 skip, refactor. 9: ask Maria."
8. WHAT GETS RECORDED, kept small on purpose (his complaint was a graph with too much in it): one dated change per EXPLAINED change, not per commit, marked as recalled, carrying the commit ids; a Decision when the answer is a choice ("File menu, not toolbar, because of accidental clicks"); a need when the answer names one ("export timestamps are UTC", source: the auditors' system). "Skip/refactor" records nothing but the coverage count. "Ask Maria" becomes a question assigned to her. "Don't know" is recorded as unknown, once, so it is never asked again.
   ⭐ AND THE FENCES GET A RULE. When the answer is "never undo this because…", it is written as a design rule on that feature ("the export button stays out of the toolbar"), because that is the sentence a future agent most needs to meet.
9. READ-BACK. Three lines: the feature's why-story in his words. He corrects it; the correction is the record.
10. COVERAGE, EVERY SESSION: "Export: 12 of 37 changes explained, 21 skipped as noise or refactor, 1 waiting on Maria, 3 left. Overall: 4 of 180 user-visible features, 60 of 640 changes." The cursor is saved; the next session resumes on the next feature.

── WHAT MAKES IT WORK AT THIS SIZE ──
· TOKENS GO WHERE THE ANSWERS ARE. No model of the whole codebase; code read only for the feature on the table; diffs opened only when a one-line summary is ambiguous. The expensive work (grouping, noise, churn) is scripted.
· HIS TIME IS THE BUDGET, and the device is the page: one reply answers ten to fifteen changes. At a few pages per session, the 20–30 features with the most history take a few weeks of half-hour sessions. The long tail may never be done, and the coverage line says so plainly.
· ASYNC IS NATURAL. A page is a list of numbered questions with guesses. It can be a document he fills in when he has ten minutes, and the agent records it later. Colleagues' pages go to them the same way.

── THE PAYOFF, AND THE GAP IN IT ──
The point is not the record; it is that the NEXT agent meets the why before it changes the code. Today reflow2 delivers a lesson at the moment a reflow2 TOOL is about to be used (req:a-lesson-is-served-at-the-step-it-concerns). It has NOTHING that delivers a PROJECT's reasons when an agent is about to change a FILE. The pieces exist in parts: the recorded whys hang off capabilities that point at directories, and tools/impact_of_diff.py already maps a diff to the capabilities and requirements it reaches — but only when someone runs it. Closing that loop (a pending change, or the file an agent opens, brings up the decisions and fence rules on its feature) is what turns /why from an archive into protection. It is a separate piece of work, and without it the walkthrough above produces a well-kept record that agents may never read.

── WHAT CAN GO WRONG, recorded beside it ──
· FATIGUE. A bazillion is still a bazillion; the skill must stop when he says, and say what is left, not push.
· MEMORY DISAGREES WITH THE MESSAGE. When he recalls something the commit message contradicts, both are kept, and his is marked recalled.
· CHANGES FROM PEOPLE WHO HAVE LEFT. Some whys are gone. "Unknown" is an honest answer and ends the question.
· FEATURES ACROSS REPOS. On a multi-repo system each repo's design holds its own whys; the hub holds the cross-cutting ones (the hub-as-client model).
· THE GRAPH SWELLS AGAIN. Guard: only explained changes, decisions, needs and fence rules are written; no structure, no per-commit records, no file checksums unless he asks.
properties.name: DECIDED 2026-09-23 — /why: one skill with two walks (why does this exist, why did it change) reads the commit history for WHAT changed and records the owner's WHY as recalled
